# Get the population data you need

`tarr.pop` helps you retrieve population counts for selected places,
years, and demographic groups. You can return those counts as a data
frame or tibble for analysis, reporting, or plotting. This guide follows
one example: obtaining population estimates for Dallas and Tarrant
counties for 2015–2018 using the small example cube included with the
package.

The usual workflow is to open a population cube, inspect its labels,
select the population you need, and convert the result to a table. If
you want totals rather than separate demographic groups, you sum those
groups before conversion. You do not need to understand the underlying R
classes to follow these steps.

A population cube is an array with named dimensions. A cell might
contain the number of female residents of Tarrant County aged 65 in 2018
in a particular race/ethnicity category. The dimension labels identify
which population each count describes. The package keeps that structure
and its metadata together while you select and summarize data.

# Find and open a cube

## Load the bundled example

The package includes a small Texas Demographic Center (TDC) county
estimates cube. You can run this guide with an installed copy of
`tarr.pop`; no download or external cube-folder setup is needed.

```{r libraries}
#| message: false
library(tarr.pop)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)
```

Use `system.file()` to find the data inside the installed package, then
pass its path to `open_poparray()`:

```{r open_tdc_estimates}
example_path <- system.file("extdata", "tdc_example.h5", package = "tarr.pop")
stopifnot(nzchar(example_path))
pop <- open_poparray(filepath = example_path)
pop
```

Opening reads the labels and metadata and creates a disk-backed view.
It does not load every population value into memory. This example contains
Dallas, Denton, and Tarrant counties and the years 2015–2018. We will
compare Dallas and Tarrant.

TDC uses one combined `race.eth` dimension for race and Hispanic ethnicity.
Other sources may use separate dimensions, so always inspect the cube you
open. For larger data collections, `set_cube_path()` configures an external
cube folder and `open_poparray()` can open a registered series by name.
Those steps are not needed for this bundled example.

## Inspect coverage and labels

Start with the source notes and available coordinates. These operations
inspect metadata without extracting population values.

```{r inspect_cube}
source_meta(pop)
names(dimnames(pop))
dim(pop)

head(times(pop))
head(areas(pop))
head(ages(pop))
sexes(pop)
dim_labels(pop, "race.eth")
```

`times()` and `areas()` return the labels for the time and area
roles. `ages()` and `sexes()` are convenient ways to inspect demographic
labels. Use `dim_labels()` for any named dimension, such as `race.eth`.
The dimensions here are `year`, `area.name`, `sex`, `age.char`, and
`race.eth`.

# Handle the 2016–2017 category change

A **schema** is the set of categories used to report the data. TDC changed
both age and race/ethnicity categories in 2017. Through 2016, ages end at
`"85 +"` (everyone aged 85 or older). From 2017, ages 85–94 are reported
individually, followed by `"95 +"`. Asian residents were included in
`"other"` through 2016 and reported separately as `"asian"` from 2017.

The cube contains the combined list of labels from both periods. That
does not mean every label applies in every year. For example, the absence
of a separate Asian count in 2016 does not mean there were no Asian
residents. Likewise, removing `"85 +"` from all years would remove the
older population from 2015 and 2016.

This example file does not yet record which labels apply in each period.
The following setup adds that information to our R object using the known
TDC reporting rules. For cubes that already have this **applicability**
metadata, inspect it and skip this setup. Do not infer reporting rules
just from missing counts.

```{r describe_reporting_periods}
semantics <- dim_semantics(pop)
semantics$age.char@applicability <- list(
  by = "year",
  schemas = list(
    list(from = "2015", through = "2016",
         levels = c("< 1", as.character(1:84), "85 +")),
    list(from = "2017", through = "2018",
         levels = c("< 1", as.character(1:94), "95 +"))
  )
)
semantics$race.eth@applicability <- list(
  by = "year",
  schemas = list(
    list(from = "2015", through = "2016",
         levels = c("black", "hispanic", "other", "white")),
    list(from = "2017", through = "2018",
         levels = c("asian", "black", "hispanic", "other", "white"))
  )
)
dim_semantics(pop) <- semantics
```

`by = "year"` means that the year determines which categories apply.
The `from` and `through` endpoints are inclusive. This changes metadata
on `pop`; it does not rewrite the packaged HDF5 file or change its counts.
The package can now sum the appropriate categories for each year while
keeping genuinely missing counts as missing.

# Select your population

Suppose we want Dallas and Tarrant counties for all four available
years. Select places and years first:

```{r select_counties_and_years}
target_counties <- c("Dallas", "Tarrant")
example_years <- times(pop)

pop_small <- pop |>
  dplyr::filter(
    area.name %in% target_counties,
    year %in% example_years
  )

pop_small
```

Here, `filter()` selects labels along cube dimensions. It keeps all
combinations of the selected coordinates; it is not yet filtering rows
of a table. For another question, you could also select particular sex,
age, or race/ethnicity labels. Each filtering expression should refer to
one dimension.

Filtering is lazy: it creates a smaller view without extracting the
population values. Compare the number of cells before and after
selection:

```{r selection_sizes}
c(original_cells = length(pop), selected_cells = length(pop_small))
```

You now have two choices. Keep the demographic detail if you need one
row for each group, or collapse those dimensions if you need county
totals.

# Choose detail or totals, then return a table

## Keep demographic detail

When you want separate demographic groups, convert the filtered cube
directly. For example, this produces a tibble for female residents in
one selected county and year, retaining age and race/ethnicity
categories:

```{r detailed_table}
selected_groups <- pop_small |>
  dplyr::filter(
    area.name == "Tarrant",
    year == example_years[length(example_years)],
    sex == "female"
  )

# EAGER: read this selected result into memory.
detail_tbl <- tibble::as_tibble(selected_groups)
head(detail_tbl)
```

There is one row per selected cube cell, with one column for each
dimension and a value column named `population` in this series.
Dimension labels may be factors, including ordered factors for age and
time. Missing counts remain missing; an `NA` does not mean zero.
Conversion preserves the cube's categories, so an overlapping category
may still appear in this detailed table. Do not sum its rows
indiscriminately.

## Calculate county totals safely

For county totals, sum over age, sex, and the combined race/ethnicity
classification. First check whether the selected categories overlap:

```{r inspect_overlap}
overlaps(pop_small)
```

The overlap report lists `"85 +"` because the complete age-label list
also includes individual older ages. With the period metadata above,
those labels are never used together in a sum. Keep `"85 +"` for the
earlier years and let `collapse_all()` use each year's applicable labels.
There is no need to remove an age group or turn off the safety checks.

Now sum over age, race/ethnicity, and sex:

```{r county_totals}
pop_totals <- pop_small |>
  collapse_all(dim = c("age.char", "race.eth", "sex"))

pop_totals
```

Collapsing reads and sums values in blocks and writes a new HDF5-backed
result. It is bounded-memory computation, rather than another queued
filter. The time and area dimensions remain, while each collapsed
dimension has one level called `"all"`.

## Choose a data frame or tibble

Both conversions below are **eager**: they read the selected result into
R memory. That is why we first selected the relevant counties and years
and, for totals, collapsed the demographic detail.

```{r convert_totals}
county_df <- as.data.frame(pop_totals)
county_tbl <- tibble::as_tibble(pop_totals)
county_tbl
```

Both tables contain the same population values. Choose a data frame for
base R tools or a tibble for a tidyverse workflow. With two counties
and four years, the total table contains eight rows. The `sex`, `age.char`,
and `race.eth` columns contain `"all"`, recording the dimensions that
were summed.

For reporting, keep just the columns you need and convert the year
labels to integers. Convert through character so factor codes are not
mistaken for years:

```{r reporting_table}
county_tbl <- county_tbl |>
  dplyr::select(year, area.name, population) |>
  dplyr::mutate(year = as.integer(as.character(year)))

county_tbl
```

At this point you have an ordinary in-memory table. You can join it to
other analysis data, write it to a file, or plot it using your usual R
tools.

# Compare age or race groups across the change

County totals are comparable because all residents are included in both
periods. For an age-specific comparison, use a common age grouping.
`group_ages()` can retain the earlier `"85 +"` count and sum the later
individual ages 85–94 plus `"95 +"` to obtain the same 85-and-older group:

```{r common_age_groups}
pop_age_groups <- pop_small |>
  group_ages(c("0-84", "85+")) |>
  collapse_all(dim = c("race.eth", "sex"))

# EAGER: read only the small grouped result for display.
age_tbl <- tibble::as_tibble(pop_age_groups)
age_tbl
```

The output labels may include spaces, such as `"85 +"`. Age groups are
interpreted as intervals, not by matching their spelling. You cannot
recover a separate 90-and-older count for 2015 or 2016 from the broader
85-and-older count. Requesting such a group produces a warning and `NA`
for the years where it cannot be derived.

For race/ethnicity comparisons, keep the meaning consistent too. One
option is to combine `"asian"` and `"other"` in the later years to match
the earlier `"other"` category:

```{r common_race_groups}
pop_race_groups <- pop_small |>
  collapse_dim(
    dim = "race.eth",
    groups = list(
      "Asian and other" = c("asian", "other"),
      "Black" = "black",
      "Hispanic" = "hispanic",
      "White" = "white"
    )
  ) |>
  collapse_all(dim = c("age.char", "sex"))

# EAGER: display the selected, summarized counts.
race_tbl <- tibble::as_tibble(pop_race_groups)
race_tbl
```

The period metadata makes the first group use only `"other"` in
2015–2016 and `"asian"` plus `"other"` in 2017–2018. It cannot split the
earlier `"other"` count into its Asian and non-Asian components. Avoid
using `sum(..., na.rm = TRUE)` as a shortcut for handling this change:
missing reporting categories and genuinely missing counts have different
meanings.

# Plot the result

```{r plot_totals}
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 4.8
ggplot(county_tbl, aes(x = year, y = population, color = area.name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Population estimates for Dallas and Tarrant counties",
    subtitle = paste("Texas Demographic Center;", paste(range(county_tbl$year), collapse = "–")),
    x = "Year",
    y = "Population",
    color = "County"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

# How the package protects your results

The object opened above is a `poparray`. It combines an array of
population values with dimension labels, source notes, time and area
roles, and semantic metadata. DelayedArray supports deferred operations,
while HDF5Array provides disk-backed storage. Keeping the large source
cube on disk and extracting only your analysis slice avoids unnecessary
memory use.

A dimension's `DimSemantics` metadata describes two separate properties.
Its partition type says whether categories are mutually exclusive or may
overlap. Its scale type says how labels should be interpreted: for
example, age groups have interval meaning rather than being arbitrary
strings. Those properties help the package reject unsafe aggregation.

```{r inspect_semantics}
time_role(pop)
area_role(pop)
dim_semantics(pop)$age.char
```

These checks cannot replace understanding the source. A metadata
definition marked as validated does not certify every count or make
every sum safe. TDC's combined race/ethnicity classification is
different from separate race and ethnicity dimensions. Likewise, Census
counts, annual estimates, and projections answer different questions.
For decennial data, years such as 2000, 2010, and 2020 are observation
years, not annual coverage.

# Where to go next

Use this workflow for your next question: choose the source, inspect its
coverage, select your places and groups, decide whether to retain detail
or calculate totals, then extract a table. Keep population values on
disk until you need them, and review overlap warnings before summing.

For more detail, see the [API reference](api_reference.qmd), the
[`poparray` class guide](poparray_class.Rmd), or the [projection
introduction](poparray_projection_intro.Rmd). Function help such as
`?dim_labels`, `?filter.poparray`, and `?collapse_all` provides argument
details and examples.
